lessons.title: Order Book Reconstruction — Building a Local Copy of the Market

children.text: The order book a trading strategy actually reacts to does not live at the exchange. It lives in the firm's own memory, rebuilt tick by tick from a raw event stream, and it is only ever as correct as the code that built it.
Market by Price vs Market by Order

markDefs.definition: A market data feed granularity that identifies every individual resting order at every price level, rather than just the aggregated total quantity at each price.

children.text: Even within tick-by-tick feeds, exchanges offer different levels of detail. A market by price feed aggregates all resting orders at a given price into a single quantity, the same view a retail trading app shows. A

feed goes further, identifying every individual order at every price level, so a firm can see exactly which order is first in line at the best price, and therefore exactly whose order would be filled next under price-time priority.

body.caption: Market by price vs market by order

cells: Aggregated quantity at each price level
Most traders, standard charting and analytics tools
Every individual order at every price level, in priority order
HFT strategies that need to know exact fill priority

children.text: Replaying Events to Build the Book

Building a local order book means starting from a known state, either an empty book at the start of the trading session or a snapshot taken mid-session, and then replaying every subsequent tick-by-tick message in exact sequence: a new order added, an existing order modified or cancelled, or a trade executed against a resting order. Each message is a small, mechanical instruction. Apply enough of them, in the right order, and the local copy matches the exchange's own book exactly.

body.title: Replay the Tape
body.scenario: A stock's order book starts empty. Four tick-by-tick messages arrive in this exact order: (1) New buy order, 100 shares at ₹500.00. (2) New buy order, 200 shares at ₹500.00. (3) New sell order, 150 shares at ₹500.00, which trades immediately against the resting buy orders at that price, since the sell order's price matches the best bid. (4) The first buy order, the original 100-share order, is cancelled.
body.prompt: After all four messages are applied, what does the book show at the ₹500.00 price level, and why?
body.modelAnswer: After messages 1 and 2, the ₹500.00 level holds 300 shares resting on the buy side: 100 from order 1, 200 from order 2. Message 3's incoming 150-share sell order matches against the buy side at that price. Price-time priority fills the earliest resting order first, so it consumes all 100 shares of order 1, then 50 of order 2's 200 shares, leaving order 2 with 150 shares remaining and the ₹500.00 level now showing 150 shares. Message 4 then tries to cancel order 1, but order 1 was already fully filled in message 3, so there is nothing left to cancel, and the book is unaffected by message 4. Final state: ₹500.00 shows 150 shares resting, all belonging to order 2.

body.text: Real feed handlers have to handle exactly this kind of edge case: a cancel message arriving for an order that has already been fully filled. Handling it incorrectly, for example by trying to remove quantity that no longer exists in memory, is a classic order book reconstruction bug, not a theoretical curiosity.

children.text: Why This Has to Be Fast Too

Book reconstruction is not a background bookkeeping task. It sits directly inside the tick-to-trade path from Chapter 1's latency budget, between the raw market data packet arriving and the strategy logic deciding whether to act. A firm that has invested in kernel bypass and an FPGA front end, from Chapter 3, gains nothing if the software maintaining its local order book uses a slow data structure, like a naive linked list that has to be walked from the front every time a price level is touched, instead of a structure built for constant-time access to the levels that matter most.

body.label: Typical Book Data Structure
body.value: Price-indexed array or similar constant-time structure
body.context: Chosen so that updating or reading a specific price level does not require scanning the rest of the book, keeping book maintenance itself inside the tick-to-trade latency budget.

body.text: An order book reconstruction bug does not crash your system. It quietly gives your strategy a wrong picture of the market, and a wrong picture executed at nanosecond speed is still wrong, just faster.

points: Market by price (MBP) feeds show aggregated quantity per price level, while market by order (MBO) feeds identify every individual order, letting a strategy know exact fill priority.
A local order book is built by replaying tick-by-tick messages, in exact sequence, from a known starting state, whether an empty book or a snapshot.
Edge cases like a cancel message arriving for an already-filled order are common and have to be handled correctly, not assumed away.
Book reconstruction sits inside the tick-to-trade latency budget from Chapter 1, so the data structure used to hold the book matters as much as the network and hardware choices from Chapter 3.
